AGENDA 
 
MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION LEGISLATION 
 
November 10, 2026 5:30 p.m.  
Committee Members O’Connell, Parr, Smith,   Aldermanic Chambers  
Superintendent (or designee) and Rep. Suzanne Chretien City Hall, 3 rd Floor 
Student Members:  Jennifer Mugisha (MHS)  
 
1. Chair O’Connell calls the meeting to order.  
 
2. The Clerk calls the roll.  
 
3. Public Forum 
 
4. Chair O’Connell advises that the purpose of the public forum is to give the residents of 
Manchester the opportunity to address the board on items of concerns affecting the community; 
each person will be given only one opportunity to speak; comments shall be limited to three 
minutes to allow all participants the opportunity to speak and any comments must be directed 
to the Chair. Speakers may offer comments on school operations and programs that concern 
them.  
 
5. Chair O’Connell advises that if there was no one else present wishing to speak, a motion would 
be in order to take all comments under advisement and further to receive and file any written 
documentation presented.    
 
6.  Update on HB1300 and November election.   
 
7.  Possible bills to advocate at state and federal levels    
 
 
8. TABLED ITEMS 
 
 
9.   NEW BUSINESS 
 
 
10. ADJOURNMENT 
  
If there is no further business, a motion is in order to adjourn. 
 
 
Per the Strategic Plan, our Mission objective is to provide a transformational learning experience and ensure that every MSD learner has high 
quality postsecondary options to attain a technical certificate, gainful employment, and/or a two-year or four-year degree.  
 
 
It is the policy of the Manchester Board of School Committee, in its actions, and those of its employees, that there shall be no discrimination on the basis 
of age, sex, race, color, marital status, physical or mental disability, religious creed, national origin or sexual orientation for employment in, or operation 
and administration of any program or activity in the Manchester School District.  The Title IX Coordinator is Dr. Kelly Espinola for staff and students.
JOINT PRE-ELECTION MEMORANDUM 
 
TO:  New Hampshire Election Officials 
FROM:  Attorney General’s Office and Secretary of State’s Office 
RE:  2026 State General Election Guidance and Issues 
DATE:  October 21, 2026 
 
 
 
Dear New Hampshire Election Officials, 
 
 
The Granite State has a rich history of secure, transparent, and trustworthy elections with high 
voter turnouts.  The quality of our elections is a direct result of each and every one of you showing 
up year after year to help Granite Staters honor their civic duty. 
 
This pre-election memorandum will highlight several reminders and useful tips. Please give it a 
read before the election and reach out to the Secretary of State’s Office if you have questions.  
We anticipate issuing additional guidance to recap voter registration and voter identity 
requirements ahead of the election. 
 
As always, thank you for serving in this role and taking part in what will be another successful 
election season. 
 
 
David M. Scanlan – Secretary of State 
 
John M. Formella – Attorney General

I. OmniBallot Accessible Voting System 
A. Pre-Election: Set Up and Test Your OmniBallot Device  
 
Set up and test the OmniBallot accessible voting device prior to election day. This includes 
connecting the printer and printing three test ballots. DO NOT wait until election day to test the 
device. 
 
For towns and cities that use electronic ballot counting devices, test your OmniBallot tablet when 
you test your electronic ballot counting device, which must be tested no later than the 
Wednesday immediately prior to the election. RSA 656:42, VIII(e)(8). The three test ballots are 
used as part of your test deck when testing your ballot counting devices.  
 
Note: during the month of October, Democracy Live has been distributing new keyboards to each 
jurisdiction for voters to use with the OmniBallot device. Please make sure you make these 
available on election day and do not forget them. 
 
B. Election Day: Test OmniBallot Device Before the Polls Open 
 
Turn on and test the device by printing one test ballot before the polls open. We strongly 
encourage you to have at least five election officials use the OmniBallot device to cast their 
ballot, which helps ensure that all ballots cast using the device remain secret even if only a few 
voters use the OmniBallot during the election. 
 
Check the system throughout the day to ensure it remains on. If you have technical problems in 
setting up or testing the device, review the OmniBallot instructions or call Democracy Live. If any 
problem is experienced while a voter is present, call the Election Division Help Desk promptly: 
(603) 271-8241. 
 
The OmniBallot device can be used by any voter upon request; DO NOT ask any voter to disclose 
whether they have a disability or what it might be.  
II. Poll Observers 
 
A. New Hampshire Elections Are Open to the Public 
 
All members of the public are allowed to attend and observe New Hampshire elections. This can 
include residents & non-residents, partisan observers, organizational observers, congressional 
observers, federal government observers, and even observers from foreign nations. 
 
During the State Primary, fewer than a dozen federal officials (most of whom were attorneys) 
wearing plain clothes were sent to observe polling locations in Nashua and Manchester wards.
2026 General Election Joint Memorandum 
Page 4 of 8 
Beyond announcing their presence when they arrived, these officials did not speak to or interact 
with any voters or election officials. No issues were reported. 
 
Our offices do not anticipate the general election will be different. That said, we have received 
many questions from election officials and members of the public regarding what observers can 
and cannot do at the polls. Therefore, we have included a few topics below to remind you of the 
general rules of the road. 
 
B. Positioning Observers within Polling Place 
 
All observers must stay outside the guardrail. New Hampshire law specifies that “[n]o person 
other than representatives of the secretary of state, representatives of the attorney general, the 
election officers, the voters admitted or those admitted to aid a voter pursuant to RSA 659:20 
shall be permitted within the guardrail except by the authority of the election officers and, then, 
only for the purpose of keeping order and enforcing the law.” RSA 659:21. Federal observers—no 
matter their agency or role—are not New Hampshire election officers. See RSA 652:14 (defining 
“election officer” for New Hampshire elections). 
 
All observers must also remain at least six feet from ballot clerk stations (RSA 659:13-a), and at 
least five feet from voter registration stations (RSA 654:7-c). During vote counting and tabulation, 
no ballot may be placed within four feet of the guardrail (RSA 659:63). 
 
C. Prohibited Acts 
 
No person may commit any of the following acts: 
 
• Intimidate Election Officials.  
o New Hampshire law specifies that no person shall use or threaten force, violence, or 
any tactic of coercion or intimidation to knowingly discourage, interfere with, or 
compel any election officer and other appointed individuals assisting at the polling 
place, such as ballot clerks and greeters, from engaging in or completing duties 
related to an election. Doing so is a crime. RSA 659:40-b. 
 
• Interfere with Voters. 
o New Hampshire law says that individuals cannot interfere or attempt to interfere with 
any voter when the voter is within the guardrail. They also cannot endeavor to induce 
any voter before voting to show how he marks or has marked his ballot. Doing either of 
these things is a crime. RSA 659:37. 
 
• Bribe, Intimidate, or Suppress Voters. 
o New Hampshire law provides that no person shall: 
 Directly or indirectly bribe any person not to register to vote or any voter not to 
vote or to vote for or against any question submitted to voters or to vote for or 
against any ticket or candidate for office at any election; or
2026 General Election Joint Memorandum 
Page 5 of 8 
 Use or threaten force, violence, or any tactic of coercion or intimidation to 
knowingly induce or compel any other person to vote or refrain from voting, 
vote or refrain from voting for any particular candidate or ballot measure, or 
refrain from registering to vote; or 
 Engage in voter suppression by knowingly attempting to prevent or deter 
another person from voting or registering to vote based on fraudulent, 
deceptive, misleading, or spurious grounds or information. This includes 
challenging another person’s right to register/vote based on information known 
to be false/misleading, or attempting to induce another person to refrain from 
registering/voting by providing the person with information known to be 
false/misleading, or attempting to induce another person to refrain from 
registering/voting by providing the person with information known to be 
false/misleading related to the date, time, place, or manner of the election.  
 Doing any of the above bullets is a crime. RSA 659:40, IV. 
 
• Tamper with electronic ballot counting devices.  
o New Hampshire law says that individuals cannot take away, tamper with, injure, 
attempt to injure, destroy, or attempt to destroy any electronic ballot counting device 
for the counting of ballots to be used or being used in an election; prevent or attempt 
to prevent the correct operation of such device; tamper with software used in the 
counting of ballots or design such software so as to cause incorrect tabulation of the 
ballots; or possess unlawfully a key to an electronic ballot counting device. Doing any 
of these is a crime. RSA 659:42. 
 
D. Call the New Hampshire Attorney General’s Office to Report Violations 
 
If you observe any person violate the rules above, please call the Attorney General’s election 
hotline at 866-868-3703. 
III. Counting, Tabulation, and Reconciliation 
 
A. Staffing for Hand Counting and Reconciliation 
 
Anticipate needing additional staff after the polls close. Recruit those working during the day 
to stay or recruit fresh individuals who can be sworn in as assistant election officials who will 
help with hand counting ballots, counting voters marked as voting on the checklist, and other 
reconciliation tasks. It is better to be able to send folks home early after the reconciliation is 
done, rather than not have enough help to complete essential tasks. 
 
Additionally, moderators in towns and wards that use ballot counting devices should anticipate a 
larger than usual number of ballots that will either need to be hand counted or have write-in
2026 General Election Joint Memorandum 
Page 6 of 8 
votes. This is in part because voters in electronic ballot counting device towns can now request 
their ballots be hand counted. 
 
B. Reconciliation 
 
You are required to conduct reconciliation on election night using the post election certificate, 
which involves: (1) tallying the total number of voters checked off on the checklist as having voted 
and (2) comparing it to (i) the total number of ballots received and cast, and (ii) the total of all 
votes counted for selected offices. 
 
Reconciliation helps the Moderator confirm that, on election night, the number of voters, ballots 
cast, and votes are equivalent. Reconciliation helps confirm that no counting or number 
transposition errors occurred while determining the total votes received by each candidate. 
Discrepancies must be announced when the results are announced. 
C. Return of Votes 
 
Remember to complete both sides of the return of votes. During the primary, the Secretary of 
State’s Office had to contact numerous towns that did not complete undervotes, overvotes, and 
the complete write in results on the back side of the return of votes. Please remember to 
complete all required information so that we do not have to track it down after the election! 
IV. HB 1300 Ballot Question 
 
The question required by HB 1300 will be printed on the ballot of every town and ward. 
The first sentence of the ballot question is “Shall the [name of municipality] limit property tax 
growth for [name(s) of school district(s)] under RSA 32:5-i?” The final sentence of paragraph V 
provides “Towns and wards serving more than one school district shall include the names of all 
such school districts in the question.” For towns and wards that are served by more than one 
school district, there will be a single ballot question that lists every school district. 
 
A. Tabulating & Reporting Results 
 
Town and ward moderators are responsible for tabulating and announcing results of all 
races and questions on the state general election ballot. The HB 1300 ballot question will be 
listed on the return of votes, on which the number of affirmative votes, the number of negative 
votes, the number of overvotes, and the number of undervotes will be reported. See RSA 659:73. 
 
In addition, RSA 32:5-i, VI (a)-(b) requires each town and ward moderator to report the 
results of the ballot question to the SAU board for each school district and SAU serving the town
2026 General Election Joint Memorandum 
Page 7 of 8 
or ward. Each SAU must thereafter certify the results of the votes to the New Hampshire 
Department of Revenue Administration. See RSA 32:5-i, VI(c). 
 
B. Vote Threshold to Pass 
 
The ballot question provides that “Adoption of the ballot question requires a three-fifths 
(3/5) majority vote.” RSA 32:5-i, V. The statute provides that the local tax cap will be adopted “[i]f 
a 3/5 majority of the voters voting in the municipalities and wards served by the school district 
approve the question.” RSA 32:5-i, VI(a).  
 
For school districts and SAUs that include more than one town or city ward, adoption of 
the ballot question requires a three-fifths (3/5) majority of the combined results of every town 
and city ward in the school district or SAU. 
 
The ballot question will only be adopted if 3/5 of the voters approve the question. 
Approval requires 3/5 of the voters who voted “yes” or “no” on the question and does not count 
any voter who cast an overvoted ballot (marking both “yes” and “no” for the question) and who 
cast an undervoted ballot (marking neither “yes” nor “no”). In other words, the total number of 
“yes” and “no” votes added together will serve as the denominator when determining whether or 
not the 3/5 approval has been achieved.  
 
For example, consider a situation where 110 ballots are cast, and the results are 
determined to be 61 votes in the affirmative, 39 votes in the negative, and 10 undervotes. For the 
purposes of calculating the 3/5, the 10 undervotes would not be counted toward the calculation. 
The numerator would be 61 votes for “yes” and the denominator would be 100 (the combined 
sum of the “yes” and “no” votes). In this scenario, the affirmative vote would exceed the 3/5 
threshold, and the measure would be approved.   
 
C. Recounts 
 
If the school administrative unit is requested to recount the ballot question for a school 
administrative unit fixed cap, the school administrative unit shall schedule and conduct a 
recount. See RSA 32:5-i, VII. If the school district is requested to recount the ballot question for a 
school district local tax cap, the school district shall schedule and the school board shall 
conduct a recount. Id.  
 
D. Timing of Recount 
 
RSA 32:5-i, VII requires recounts on the ballot question to be conducted no earlier than 5 
days and no later than 10 days after a petition for recount is received. However, if any 
municipality’s ballots are subject to a ballot question recount under RSA 32:5-i, VII and a state
2026 General Election Joint Memorandum 
Page 8 of 8 
recount under RSA chapter 660, the Secretary of State shall conduct any state recounts before 
any school administrative unit or school board conducts a ballot question recount. Any ballot 
question recounts involving those ballots shall be conducted no earlier than 5 days and no later 
than 10 days after the state recount of those ballots has been completed. 
 
E. Custody of Ballots 
 
Each municipal clerk’s office having possession of ballots that will be recounted under 
RSA 32:5-i, VII must deliver those ballots to the school board or school administrative unit on the 
date and time of the recount. If any ballots were the subject of a state recount under RSA chapter 
660, the Secretary of State’s Office shall be responsible for delivering those ballots to the school 
board or school administrative unit on the date and time of any subsequent ballot question 
recount. At the conclusion of the ballot question recount, each municipal clerk’s office must 
retrieve that municipality’s ballots to be preserved at the clerk’s office pursuant to RSA chapter 
659. 
 
F. HB 130 Legislative History 
 
The Secretary of State’s Office has added to its website the full legislative history of HB 
1300.  The page can be accessed directly here: HB 1300 Ballot Question | New Hampshire 
Secretary of State. There is also a link to the page from the SOS homepage (Welcome | New 
Hampshire Secretary of State) under “Happening Now.”  The legislative history is one resource 
that voters can turn to if they have question about HB 1300. 
 
V. Constitutional Question Voter’s Guide 
 
The legislature included language for a voter’s guide for the constitutional question regarding 
registers of probate.  However, the Secretary of State’s Office did not receive authorization to 
print and distribute the voter’s guide.  See RSA 663:3-a. 
 
If you get questions regarding the constitutional question, you may direct them to the text of the 
voter’s guide adopted in CACR 13 
(https://gc.nh.gov/bill_status/pdf.aspx?id=30183&q=billVersion).  
 
Voters' Guide.  
AT THE PRESENT TIME, the constitution references registers of probate while the 
office's duties were redistributed to circuit court clerks in 2011.  
IF THE AMENDMENT IS ADOPTED, the constitution will eliminate the position of 
register of probate
